PROBLEM DEFINITIONS (the SOURCE and TARGET docstrings from problems.py, complete as given here):

SOURCE = ThreeSat
3-SAT.

Instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[l1, l2, l3], ...]}
  * Variables are 1..m. A literal is +v (v is true) or -v (v is false).
  * Every clause has exactly 3 literals on 3 different variables, so a
    clause may not repeat a variable or contain both v and -v.
  * Literal order inside a clause and clause order do not matter. The
    same clause may appear more than once.
  * Variables need not all appear in a clause.

Yes iff some assignment of true/false to variables 1..m makes every
clause contain at least one true literal.

Edge cases: a formula with no clauses is satisfiable (yes), for any m,
including m = 0. A formula with clauses needs m >= 3.

TARGET = Clique
Clique.

Instance: {"n": n, "edges": [[u, v], ...], "k": k}
  * Vertices are 0..n-1. Edges are undirected pairs [u, v] with u != v;
    [u, v] and [v, u] are the same edge and may not both appear.
  * k is any integer.

Yes iff the graph has a clique of AT LEAST k vertices: k vertices with an
edge between every two of them.

Edge cases: k <= 0 is always yes. k = 1 is yes whenever n >= 1. k > n is
always no.

WORKING DIRECTORY: /tmp/reduction-uqhv2trl

The answer to the returned instance must be yes exactly when the answer to the input instance is yes, and reduce must run in polynomial time. Do not call the brute-force solvers inside reduce.

{"command":"cd /tmp/reduction-uqhv2trl && cat <<'EOF' > reduce.py
"""Polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT to Clique.

Standard gadget reduction:

  * For every clause i and every one of its three literals, create a vertex.
    Clause i owns the three vertices 3*i, 3*i+1, 3*i+2.
  * Join two vertices with an edge iff they belong to different clauses and
    their literals are not complementary (i.e. not one the negation of the
    other).  Vertices inside the same clause are never joined.
  * Set k = number of clauses.

A clique of size k must pick exactly one vertex from each clause (no two
vertices of a clause are adjacent) and no two picked literals contradict, so
it yields a satisfying assignment.  Conversely, a satisfying assignment lets
us pick one true literal per clause; those vertices are pairwise adjacent and
form a k-clique.  Thus the graph has a clique of size >= k iff the formula is
satisfiable.

Edge cases:
  * No clauses -> k = 0, and Clique answers yes for k <= 0, matching the
    empty (satisfiable) formula, including num_vars = 0.
  * Duplicate clauses become separate gadgets; the same literal choice can be
    reused because equal literals are adjacent across gadgets.
"""


def reduce(instance):
    """Map a 3-SAT instance to a Clique instance (yes-preserving)."""
    num_vars = instance["num_vars"]
    clauses = instance["clauses"]

    # One vertex per literal occurrence; clause i owns 3*i .. 3*i+2.
    n = 3 * len(clauses)

    edges = []
    for i in range(len(clauses)):
        for j in range(3):
            u = 3 * i + j
            a = clauses[i][j]
            for i2 in range(i + 1, len(clauses)):
                for j2 in range(3):
                    b = clauses[i2][j2]
                    # Complementary literals cannot both be true.
                    if a != -b:
                        edges.append([u, 3 * i2 + j2])

    return {"n": n, "edges": edges, "k": len(clauses)}
EOF
